lessons.title: Commodity Options in India: Options on Futures vs Options on Goods

children.text: A futures position has no ceiling on what you can lose if the price runs against you. For many traders and businesses, that is too much risk. What if you could pay a fixed amount upfront for the right to benefit if crude oil rises, and simply walk away if it does not? That is what an option offers. Since MCX launched India's first commodity options on gold in October 2017, options have become a major part of commodity trading, especially in crude oil and natural gas. By the end of this lesson you will know how commodity calls and puts work, how their payoffs are calculated in rupees, how Indian options on futures differ from options on goods, and why most cheap options expire worthless.

body.text: An option buyer pays a premium for a right, not an obligation, so the most they can lose is that premium. An option seller collects the premium and takes on the obligation, and with it a risk that can be many times larger.

children.text: Calls, Puts and the Premium

markDefs.definition: The right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying at a fixed strike price, on or before expiry depending on the option style.
The price at which the option buyer can buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying if they exercise the option.
The right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying at a fixed strike price.
The price of an option, paid by the buyer to the seller upfront. It is the buyer's maximum possible loss.

children.text: A
call option
gives the buyer the right to buy at a fixed
strike price
. A
put option
gives the buyer the right to sell at the strike. The buyer pays the seller a
premium
for that right.

cells: Price rises above strike plus premium
Price falls below strike minus premium
Large: strike minus premium, down to a price of zero

body.label: Premium is quoted per unit, not per lot
body.value: Multiply by the same factor as futures
body.context: MCX Crude Oil options are quoted in ₹ per barrel on a 100 barrel contract, so a premium of ₹180 costs ₹180 × 100 = ₹18,000 per lot. Gold options on the 1 kg contract are quoted per 10 grams, so multiply by 100.

children.text: Buying a Call: A Crude Oil Example

Karthik, a 33-year-old engineer in Bengaluru, thinks crude oil could jump if an upcoming OPEC+ meeting announces deeper cuts. Crude oil futures are at ₹6,420 per barrel. Rather than buy futures and risk an open-ended loss, he buys one lot of the ₹6,500 strike call for a premium of ₹180 per barrel (illustrative prices).

stats.label: Maximum loss
stats.context: If crude futures settle at or below ₹6,500

body.caption: Karthik's long ₹6,500 crude oil call bought at ₹180. Loss is capped at the premium below ₹6,500; profit begins above the ₹6,680 breakeven.

body.latex: \text{Long call P\&L at expiry} = \left[\max(0,\; F - K) - \text{Premium}\right] \times \text{Multiplier}
body.caption: F = final price of the underlying futures, K = strike price. For a long put, use max(0, K minus F). Multiplier = lot size ÷ quotation unit.

body.title: Karthik's payoff
body.prompt: At expiry, the crude oil futures price is ₹6,900 per barrel. What is Karthik's profit or loss on his one lot of the ₹6,500 call bought at ₹180, in rupees?
body.explanation: Intrinsic value = ₹6,900 minus ₹6,500 = ₹400. Subtract the ₹180 premium to get ₹220 per barrel. Multiply by 100 barrels: ₹22,000 profit, on an outlay of ₹18,000.

children.text: Buying a Put: Insurance for a Gold Stockist

Ramesh, a bullion trader in Zaveri Bazaar, Mumbai, holds 1 kg of gold inventory. Gold is at ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams. He is worried about a fall over the next two months, but does not want to give up the gain if gold rallies, which a futures hedge would do. So he buys a ₹1,00,000 strike put on gold for ₹1,800 per 10 grams (illustrative), costing ₹1,80,000 for the 1 kg contract.

body.caption: Ramesh's long ₹1,00,000 gold put bought at ₹1,800. It gains as gold falls below the ₹98,200 breakeven, and the most it can lose is the premium.

body.title: Ramesh's effective value per 10 grams at expiry: three choices
body.xAxisLabel: Gold price at expiry (₹ per 10 grams)

children.text: The put gives Ramesh a floor of ₹98,200 per 10 grams: the strike minus the premium. Below that, the put's gains offset his inventory losses. Above ₹1,00,000, the put expires worthless, but his gold keeps rising in value, less the ₹1,800 he paid. A futures hedge would have locked him at ₹1,00,000 in every scenario, with no cost upfront but no upside either.

body.text: Futures hedges and options hedges solve different problems. A futures hedge removes both downside and upside, at no upfront cost. An options hedge removes only the downside, but you pay for it in advance, exactly like an insurance premium.

body.title: Where does the put pay off?
body.question: Ramesh bought the ₹1,00,000 gold put for ₹1,800. Ignoring costs, below what gold price at expiry does the put make an overall profit on its own?
body.explanation: A long put breaks even at strike minus premium: ₹1,00,000 minus ₹1,800 = ₹98,200. Between ₹98,200 and ₹1,00,000 the put has some value but does not recover the full premium.

children.text: Moneyness: Where the Strike Sits

body.caption: Moneyness for calls and puts (crude futures at ₹6,420)

markDefs.definition: The amount an option is in the money: current price minus strike for a call, strike minus current price for a put, and never below zero.
The part of an option's premium above its intrinsic value, reflecting the chance of a favourable move before expiry. It decays to zero by expiry.

children.text: An option's premium has two parts.
Intrinsic value
is how much it is in the money right now.
Time value
is everything else, the price of the possibility that things move your way before expiry. OTM options are made up entirely of time value, and time value melts to zero by expiry.

body.text: Deep out-of-the-money options look cheap, which is exactly why beginners buy them. A ₹3 natural gas call can feel like a lottery ticket. But if the price never gets past strike plus premium, it expires worthless. Buying cheap OTM options repeatedly is one of the fastest ways retail traders lose money in commodity options.

children.text: Selling Options: Collecting Premium, Carrying Risk

Every option bought was sold by someone. Sellers, also called writers, receive the premium upfront and win if the option expires worthless. Because their potential loss is large, the exchange requires them to post margin, much like a futures position. Buyers pay only the premium and post no margin.

body.caption: A short ₹6,800 crude oil call sold at ₹90. The seller keeps the ₹9,000 premium if crude stays below ₹6,800, but losses grow without limit above the ₹6,890 breakeven.

body.title: Show me the math: when a short call goes wrong

children.text: A trader sells one lot of the ₹6,800 crude call for ₹90, collecting ₹9,000. A sudden supply disruption sends crude futures to ₹7,400 at expiry.
Intrinsic value owed: ₹7,400 minus ₹6,800 = ₹600 per barrel
Less premium received: ₹600 minus ₹90 = ₹510 per barrel
Loss on one lot: ₹510 × 100 = ₹51,000

The seller risked ₹51,000, and potentially much more, to earn ₹9,000. Crude oil can gap sharply on geopolitical news, often during the late evening session. Option selling is a strategy for experienced traders with strict risk controls, not for beginners.
Options on Futures vs Options on Goods

markDefs.definition: Options whose underlying is a commodity futures contract. On exercise, they turn into a position in that futures contract at the strike price.
Options whose underlying is the physical commodity itself. On exercise, they settle directly through delivery of the goods or as specified by the exchange, without creating a futures position.

children.text: Here is where Indian commodity options differ from equity options. Most MCX commodity options are
options on futures
: the underlying is not the commodity itself but a specific futures contract. SEBI has also permitted
options on goods
, where the underlying is the physical commodity, and exchanges have introduced such contracts on select commodities.

body.title: Options on futures vs options on goods

columns.label: Options on futures (most MCX options)
points: Underlying is a specific futures contract, such as the crude oil futures for a given month
Settlement price is based on that futures contract
On exercise, the option devolves into a futures position at the strike price
Expire a few days before the underlying futures contract
After devolvement, you must meet futures margin and manage the futures position

columns.label: Options on goods
points: Underlying is the physical commodity itself
Settlement references the spot or goods price defined by the exchange
On exercise, settles directly, typically through delivery of the goods, with no futures step
Expiry is linked to the delivery schedule of the goods
Exercise can mean paying full value or delivering the commodity, with taxes and logistics

children.text: How Devolvement Works

markDefs.definition: Options that can be exercised only at expiry, not before. MCX commodity options are European style, though they can be bought and sold any time before expiry.

children.text: MCX commodity options are
European style

: they are exercised only at expiry, though you can trade them at any time before that. At expiry, in-the-money options on futures are exercised automatically as per exchange rules, and devolve like this:
Long call exercised:
you get a long position in the underlying futures at the strike price.
Long put exercised:
you get a short position in the underlying futures at the strike price.
Option sellers assigned:
they get the opposite futures position at the strike price.
Then the futures rules apply:
the new position is marked to market, needs futures margin, and must be closed, rolled or taken towards that contract's own settlement.

body.text: Devolvement surprises many new traders. If you buy a gold call with ₹20,000 of premium and it expires in the money, you can wake up holding a gold futures position that requires far more margin than the premium you paid, and which may be close to its own tender period. If you do not want a futures position, square off in-the-money options before expiry.

body.title: Exercise style
body.textWithBlank: MCX commodity options can be exercised only at expiry, which makes them ___ style options.
body.explanation: European options can only be exercised at expiry. American options can be exercised any time before expiry. Either way, you can sell your option in the market before expiry to capture its value.

body.title: The ₹2 natural gas calls
body.scenario: Pooja, a 24-year-old in Jaipur, sees natural gas futures at ₹280 per mmBtu after a warm spell in the US. A trading influencer calls for "₹350 before expiry". She buys 10 lots of the ₹340 strike natural gas call at ₹2 per mmBtu, on a contract size of 1,250 mmBtu, with 8 days to expiry. "Only ₹2 each, so how much can I really lose?" she says.
body.prompt: How much has Pooja actually paid, what does natural gas need to do for her to profit, and what is the most likely outcome?
body.modelAnswer:
What she paid: ₹2 × 1,250 mmBtu = ₹2,500 per lot, and 10 lots = ₹25,000. The "₹2" is per unit, not per lot.

What needs to happen: breakeven at expiry is ₹340 + ₹2 = ₹342, which is about 22% above the current ₹280 in just 8 days. Natural gas is volatile, but that is a very large move in a very short time.

Most likely outcome: the options stay out of the money and expire worthless, losing the full ₹25,000. Deep OTM options with little time left are almost pure time value, which melts quickly.

A better approach: if she has a genuine view, consider a nearer strike with a realistic breakeven, size it so the full premium is a small share of capital, and never base a trade on an influencer target.

cards.definition: The right, not obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price.
The right, not obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price.
The price paid by the buyer to the seller; the buyer's maximum loss.
How far an option is in the money, never below zero.
Premium above intrinsic value; decays to zero by expiry.
Options whose underlying is a futures contract; exercise devolves into a futures position.
Options whose underlying is the physical commodity; exercise settles directly without a futures step.
Exercisable only at expiry, as MCX commodity options are.

points: A call is the right to buy and a put is the right to sell at the strike price. Buyers pay a premium, which is their maximum loss.
Premiums are quoted per unit, so multiply by lot size ÷ quotation unit: a ₹180 crude premium costs ₹18,000 per lot.
Long call breakeven = strike + premium. Long put breakeven = strike minus premium.
Puts work like insurance for holders; futures hedges lock both sides at no upfront cost.
Option sellers collect premium but face large, potentially unlimited losses, and must post margin.
Most MCX options are European-style options on futures that devolve into futures positions at expiry. Options on goods settle directly against the commodity.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All prices and premiums are illustrative. Contract specifications, exercise rules and the list of options on goods change over time; always check current exchange specifications. Options, and option selling in particular, carry high risk.
